In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this study found support that thwarted belongingness, perceived burdensomeness, interpersonal shame, and perfectionistic family discrepancy are associated with depression among Asian American college students.

the study found that thwarted belongingness, perceived burdensomeness, and interpersonal shame are risk factors for depression among Asian American students, but that the relationship between thwarted belongingness is moderated by perfectionistic family discrepancy.

this study found support for Joiner’s (2010) Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicidality in a sample of Asian American students, and that this theory may be useful for understanding Asian American students’ depression risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found that thwarted belongingness (feeling disconnected from others) and perceived burdensomeness (feeling like a burden) contribute to interpersonal shame and depression, especially among Asian American students who have a large gap between what their parents expect and what they can actually accomplish.
Asian American college students with perfectionistic discrepancy may be at risk for depression when they experience thwarted belongingness.
Asian American students who experience perfectionistic family discrepancy, thwarted belongingness, and perceived burdensomeness may be at a higher risk for depression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
students with perfectionism may be at higher risks for depression while experiencing interpersonal factors such as thwarted belongingness.

counselors should be aware that Asian American students may be at greater risk for depression if they experience thwarted belongingness or perceive burdensomeness and if they have perfectionistic family discrepancy.

Asian American students who experience perfectionistic family discrepancy and thwarted belongingness are at higher risk for future depression, and counselors can help these students develop skills to cope with their feelings. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2021 APA, all rights reserved)
